implementation_notes: Default .NET realization: register services on IServiceCollection and resolve them from IServiceProvider - the container is the well-known object and the service type (or keyed service name) is the key. What replaces the classic Registry class is the framework pair plus ServiceDescriptor; write a hand-rolled registry only when you need a key domain the container does not model (string-keyed plugin names with duplicate detection).
pitfalls: The provider must live as long as its consumers: capturing the root IServiceProvider inside a singleton and resolving scoped services from it is the classic captive-dependency bug (scoped services, and the provider itself, are disposed with the scope).

Registrations are not validated until you ask for them: GetRequiredService throws at resolution time, far from the misconfiguration - build the provider with validation (ValidateOnBuild/ValidateScopes) in development.
The container is a service locator when injected everywhere: resolving dependencies inside business code hides the real dependency graph.

variants.name: ConcurrentDictionary<string, Func<T>> registry
variants.implementation_notes: The hand-rolled form: a static (or injected) ConcurrentDictionary keyed by name holding factories, with TryAdd for fail-fast registration and TryGetValue plus factory invocation for lookup. It is the right realization when names are data (plugin ids, codec names) rather than service types, and it needs no framework dependency.
pitfalls: ConcurrentDictionary makes individual operations atomic, not sequences: register-then-resolve contracts, or 'register only if absent plus mutate', still need a single atomic method (TryAdd/GetOrAdd with a factory).
GetOrAdd may invoke its factory more than once under contention and the discarded value leaks if it is IDisposable.
Static state is per assembly-load-context and never cleared, so tests leak registrations; expose a reset hook or make the registry an instance.
